intro.text: Phoenix Education Partners, Inc. is the parent company of The University of Phoenix, Inc., a pioneer in online education for working adults. Founded in 1976, The University of Phoenix provides access to higher education opportunities that enable students to develop the knowledge and skills necessary to achieve their professional goals, improve the performance of their organizations and provide leadership and service to their communities.

lines.name: Cash and cash equivalents
lines.why: Cash can repay debt or be paid out: a financial asset. Cash needed to run the business is operating; move it if you know how much.

lines.name: Short-term investments
lines.why: Securities held for the cash they will return: financial.

lines.name: Long-term investments
lines.why: Securities held for their return: financial. A stake in another business that is part of operations is operating.

lines.name: Receivables
lines.why: Owed by customers for sales: operating.

lines.name: Prepaid and other current assets
lines.why: Prepayments and other operating items: operating.

lines.name: Property, plant and equipment
lines.why: Assets used to produce and sell: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets
lines.why: Leased stores, offices and equipment used in the business: operating.

lines.name: Goodwill
lines.why: Paid for acquired businesses: operating.

lines.name: Intangible assets
lines.why: Acquired technology, brands and customer relationships: operating.

lines.name: Deferred tax assets
lines.why: Taxes on operating income paid ahead: operating.

lines.name: Other non-current assets
lines.why: Other long-term operating items: operating.

lines.name: Accounts payable
lines.why: Owed to suppliers for operations: operating.

lines.name: Accrued compensation
lines.why: Wages, bonuses and benefits earned but not yet paid: operating.

lines.name: Deferred revenue
lines.why: Customers' payments ahead of delivery: operating.

lines.name: Other current liabilities
lines.why: Other operating items due within a year: operating.

lines.name: Long-term debt
lines.why: Bonds, notes and loans: financial.

lines.name: Operating lease liabilities
lines.why: Rent owed on leases used in the business: operating by default. Move it to financing to treat leases like debt (if the balance sheet has no lease line of its own, they sit inside other liabilities).

lines.name: Other non-current liabilities
lines.why: Other long-term operating obligations: operating.

lines.name: Other current assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total current assets minus the current lines above: current assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other non-current assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Non-current assets (total assets − current assets) minus the non-current lines above: assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other current liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total current liabilities minus the current lines above: current liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other non-current liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Non-current liabilities (total liabilities − current liabilities) minus the non-current lines above: liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

s.t: Our degree-granting programs represented approximately 98% of our net revenue for fiscal year 2026 and serve a diverse set of students who are seeking to improve their career opportunities:

During fiscal year 2026, 88.6% of the University’s cash basis revenue for eligible tuition and fees was derived from the receipt of federal program funds, as calculated under the 90/10 Rule described in “—Regulatory Environment—Regulation of Student Financial

• we derived 88.6% of our cash basis revenue from Title IV and other designated federal education assistance funds in our most recent fiscal year, and if the University becomes ineligible to participate in Title IV programs, including due to the “90/10 Rule,” or participation is materially limited, our business may not be sustainable;

Since we derived 88.6% of our cash basis revenue from Title IV and other designated federal education assistance funds in our most recent fiscal year, if the University becomes ineligible to participate in Title IV programs, or participation is materially limited, our sources of revenue will become significantly more restricted and our business may not be sustainable.
No individual customer accounted for more than 10 % of our consolidated net revenue in fiscal years 2026 and 2025 .
The principal source of federal student financial aid in the United States is established and governed by Title IV of the Higher Education Act and regulations promulgated thereunder.

A student’s success in obtaining licensure following graduation typically depends on several factors, including the background and qualifications of the individual graduate, whether the institution and the program were approved by the state in which the graduate seeks licensure, or by a professional association; whether the program from which the student graduated meets all requirements for professional licensure in that state; whether the institution and the program are accredited and, if so, by what accrediting commissions; and whether the institution’s degrees are recognized by other states

During litigation, the federal courts overseeing the Sweet settlement have referenced the Department of Education’s assurances that it will not rely on automatic discharges under the Sweet settlement as the basis upon which to recoup such discharged loans from institutions.
Accordingly, the Department of Education may be unable to rely on any such automatic discharges as the basis of a recoupment action against us.

In conducting oversight of the administration of the federal student aid program by Title IV-participating institutions, the Department of Education relies on compliance reviews, including program reviews conducted by Department of Education staff, mandatory annual compliance audits by independent audit firms, and audits and investigations conducted by the OIG.
We also rely on agreements under which we contract to own, or license rights to use, intellectual property developed by faculty members, content experts and other third parties.

Among other matters, these regulations govern the participation by the University in federal student financial aid programs under Title IV, which is the principal source of funding for students at the University.

Further, the federal courts overseeing Sweet have referenced the Department of Education’s assurances that it will not rely on automatic discharges of BDR claims under the Sweet settlement as the basis upon which to recoup such discharged loans from institutions.

Certain of our students require or desire professional licenses or certifications after graduation to obtain employment in their chosen fields and their success depends on several factors, including the individual merits of the student, whether the institution and the program were approved by the relevant state government or regulatory authorities, whether the student’s program meets professional licensure requirements, and whether the program is accredited in accordance with state requirements.
Our financial performance depends on our ability to develop and maintain favorable awareness of the University among, and enroll and retain, students.

Our current and future success depends on the skills, efforts, and motivation of our employees, senior management, and faculty, who generally have significant experience with our business and industry, as well as our ability to attract and retain qualified personnel.

We rely on a combination of copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets (including know-how), patents, and domain names, as well as employee and third-party confidentiality agreements, intellectual property licenses, and other contractual rights, to establish, maintain, protect and enforce our rights in our curricula and other course materials, technology, proprietary information, processes, and other assets.

Our business relies on IT networks and systems to store this data, process financial and personal information, manage a variety of business processes, and comply with regulatory, legal, and tax requirements.

We rely on third-party vendors whose service may be of lower quality than ours, whose responsiveness may be less timely than ours, and whose compliance practices may increase our operational and compliance risk.

We rely on third-party vendors to provide technology-related services to our students, including for student software systems and services related to the Title IV and financial aid program administration.

As a “controlled company” under NYSE rules and an “emerging growth company” under SEC rules and regulations, we rely on exemptions from certain corporate governance and disclosure requirements, and our stockholders will not have the same protections as stockholders of companies subject to such requirements.
We are a holding company and rely on dividends, distributions, and other payments, advances, and transfers of funds from our subsidiaries to meet our obligations.

Future dividend declarations will be at the discretion of our Board and will depend on our financial condition, cash flows, capital requirements, contractual or legal restrictions, including those under our Revolving Facility, and other factors considered relevant by our Board.
The net revenue we generate in a given period largely depends on the total number of courses taken by the enrolled student population and the price per course.
Our ability to grow profitably depends on our ability to manage our cost structure.
Our primary sources of cash are cash provided by operations and cash and cash equivalents and marketable securities on hand.
The timing and amount of any repurchases will depend on a variety of factors, including our stock price, general market conditions, liquidity and capital requirements, and other uses of cash.
We have chosen to rely on the other exemptions and reduced reporting requirements provided by the JOBS Act.

Students may fund their education using a single source or combination of sources, including loans and grants from U.S. federal financial aid programs established under Title IV of the Higher Education Act and related regulations (“Title IV”), military benefit programs, employer tuition assistance and personal funds.
The accounting for a modification of a share-based award depends on the terms and conditions of the original and modified awards.
As of August 31, 2024, Talent Mobility, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Phoenix Education Operating Corp. (“PEOC”), had a minority ownership interest in Empath, Inc. (“Empath”).
